mechanism: Oversized concrete basket versus one wage token, with an explicit long measure that turns the early shortfall into a visual question.
hypothesis: The oversized necessities basket and single wage token should communicate the film's wage-days measure more quickly than the abstract pay-versus-price paradox or the three-period timeline; the short text adds the opening 333-day stake. This is a creative hypothesis, not a CTR prediction.

script_alignment.promise: The film compares an annual reconstructed basket of basic needs with daily pay across selected London historical periods.
script_alignment.first_confirmation: Opening narration names bread, fuel, washing and light, then explains the pre-Black-Death estimate of roughly 333 paid days against a 250-day model year.
script_alignment.payoff: The film traces a rise to about 216 wage-days in 1600–1649 and later fall to about 116 in 1850–1899, with explicit limits on what the basket measures.
script_alignment.genre: Illustrated explanatory economic history; reconstructed comparison, not documentary footage of a particular family.
limits: The basket is reconstructed for a family of four and does not include all spending.
Wage-days are not a record of any worker's actual working year.
Do not imply comparison with modern prices.
